speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to a question asked yesterday on the orders of the day by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) regarding the recent regrettable air accident near Crumlin airport. His question was:
Has the minister looked into two facts which have been reported in connection with this tragedy; the first being that there was a failure of power at the airport and no indication that there were in use at that time any auxiliary or mobile lights or such other equipment; secondly, that there was a delay of more than an hour before the stretcher party arrived at the scene of the accident from the airport?
Perhaps I might first mention that it was announced yesterday that a board of inquiry would be nominated within a few days to hold a public inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the accident. I do not wish to anticipate any of the facts that may be determined by the inquiry, but should like to give the house an answer to the questions raised by the hon. member.
From information received by the department, it is understood that the airport rotating beacon and obstruction lights were in operation continuously. The runway and runway approach lights are under a separate control system which is set up so that all runway and taxiway lights, plus one set of approach lights, may be turned on at the same time. The control system, however, is not intended to carry at one time more than one set of approach lights, because experience has demonstrated that this is a necessary safety measure. If more than one set of runway approach lights are on at the same time, pilots may be confused and use the wrong runway.
At 11.49 p.m. the pilot asked for all runway and approach lights to be turned on, presumably because of the urgent situation in which he found himself. In view of the special circumstances, and in spite of the control arrangements, all lights were turned on, but they stayed on for approximately one minute only and then a fuse blew out because of the overload on the system. The traffic

control officer on duty in the tower immediately called the senior controller, the airport maintenance foreman, the field radio technician, and then called the R.C.A.F. for crash and fire trucks. Trucks and other vehicles were lined up on one side of the runway, lighting it effectively, and the pilot of the aircraft was informed by radio that this had been done. The lights were restored at 10 minutes after midnight, having been out of operation for 20 minutes.
Hon. members will note that although the runway and approach lights were not in operation, the tower still maintained ground to air radio communication with the aircraft. Also the instrument landing system and the radio range were still in operation, providing a means by which an aircraft equipped with a radio and instrument landing facilities could make an approach to landing.
With regard to auxiliary lighting, I am informed that there is auxiliary generating equipment at the field. This, however, is designed to be used in the event of a general failure in the power supply to the airport. It is not the general practice here or in any other country to instal a complete duplicate set of airport lights.
In connection with the reference to time of arrival of the stretcher party, I am advised that the tower continued in radio communication with the aircraft until approximately one minute after midnight. At 5 minutes after midnight the tower telephoned the township and provincial police and a commercial ambulance. The airport did not know at this time the exact location of the aircraft. The department does not, of course, operate an ambulance service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the traditional speech from the throne there are some matters on which I think all hon. members are in cordial agreement. There are three items to which I will refer. The first is the reference to the bringing into operation of the Disabled Persons Act, whereby assistance will be granted to totally disabled persons. Hon. members who come from the province of Ontario will be more or less familiar with this act which has been in force in Ontario for some time. I am sure all hon. members from Ontario will agree that in Ontario the act has filled a long-felt need. I trust that the contributions the federal government will make will be ample in every way.
The second matter in the speech from the throne on which I think all hon. members will agree is the provision whereby the age of eligibility for blind persons will be amended and the income ceiling will be adjusted. I am sure all hon. members are only too anxious that every possible assistance will be rendered to our more unfortunate citizens who are blind.
The third matter is the welcome announcement that the War Veterans Allowance Act will, after these long and weary years, be amended. I would say to the minister that I hope on this occasion when the act is amended he will not make the same mistake that was made several years ago when the act was amended. I wonder if the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) would mind just for a moment giving me his attention. I should like to say this to the minister. When you bring in the act to adjust the war veterans allowance, I hope you will not make the same error that was made by your predecessor several years ago when this act was amended and when you made only a slight raise in the monthly compensation and only a slight adjustment in the ceilings. At that time the veterans committee and the government were urged in every possible way by all opposition parties that the monthly allowance be placed at a higher figure than $50 a month and, further, that the ceiling be much increased over
[Mr. Pinard.l

and above the amount proposed in the act. I say that to the minister in all kindness because he realizes only too well that an act such as the War Veterans Allowance Act is only amended once in a good many years. If the same error is made this time, I fear that it will be a fairly long time before there will be any further change in this act.
I might point out to the minister that the same mistake was made by his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), when some few years ago he brought in a bill to adjust the salaries paid to the members of the judiciary. He found that he made a mistake, and now he has to come back and do the same thing all over again. Therefore on behalf of these veterans, most of them from the first world war, I urge the minister that, when it is decided in cabinet council how much the increase in the allowance is going to be, he should be very generous and keep in mind that these veterans should not be restricted with a ceiling on their income but on the other hand should be urged in every possible way to earn as much as possible for themselves and their families. I have only one other suggestion. When the bill is introduced I would ask the minister if he would consider having the increase, no matter what it may be, made retroactive to at least the 1st of January, 1955.
I have received from the county council of the county in which I reside a copy of a resolution which they have asked me to bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). The resolution passed by the council of the county of Hastings reads as follows:
That since, by the statutes of Canada, November 11th is designated as a public holiday, our government be urged to enact legislation that November 11th not only be declared a national holiday, but that it also be observed as such.
I can recall occasions in November when parliament has been in session and the House of Commons has continued to sit and conduct business just the same as any other day. There may be many in Canada who do not care or pay much attention to the significance of Armistice day, but at least to the veterans of the first war it means a great deal, and I would suggest to the government that the resolution of the county council be given attention.
It was suggested last session that at this session the Dominion Succession Duty Act would be amended, but there is no mention of it in the speech from the throne. I trust that amendments will be brought forward at this session because I am sure the government is aware of many unsatisfactory features in the present legislation. I will mention only one or two. One is that at the time the rate

of exemption was set the dollar was worth a great deal more than it is today. The other is that an estate is entitled to exemption up to $50,000 but if the estate exceeds that amount duty is collected on the whole amount. If there are to be amendments of this act I trust the legislation will be sent to a committee of the house for study and consideration. If so, there is another point that might well be considered by the minister, namely, that the exemption granted to a widow under the act should be raised considerably.
In the speech from the throne reference is made to unemployment and it is described as being only seasonal and regional. I have in my hand a long article from the Belleville Ontario-Intelligencer of January 17 which contains a long statement issued by the manager of the unemployment office at Belleville. The article is headed in large capital letters: "Employment Office Appeals to Residents to Get Repairs, Alterations of Homes Done Now." The article is two columns long. It states that in the Belleville office alone there are over 16,000 persons, male and female, registered for work. It further points out that the Belleville office does not service the whole county of Hastings, that the town of Deseronto is serviced by the Napanee office and that the west half of the township of Sidney, which contains the large town of Trenton with a population of well over 10,000, is serviced by the Trenton office. In one county there are over 16,000 registered for work, not including two large centres. Therefore I submit to the minister that it is quite reasonable to say that in the whole county of Hastings there are at least 20,000 persons registered and seeking work at the present time.
That is only one county in the province of Ontario. Yet in the speech from the throne this condition is referred to as only seasonal and regional. The legislation the minister introduced last week and the legislation he proposes to introduce with respect to unemployment insurance are all to the good, but I would repeat to the minister what many others have said to him, that these increases, beneficial as they may be, are not an answer to the problem. They do not provide jobs. The minister at least has something to say about the policy of the government. He can at least use his voice to urge a reduction in taxation and do what he can to assist industry to produce more at lower cost so that industry will be better able to face and meet the competition of goods manufactured in other countries.
Much has been said in this debate regarding the importation of cheddar cheese from
The Address-Mr. G. S. White New Zealand. In eastern Ontario where I reside the cheese industry is most important. Hastings county is the place where the famous Black Diamond cheese is manufactured, a cheese that has done a great deal to advertise Canada throughout the United States. The whole dairy industry is of great importance to the economy of Canada. I should like to point out that it is estimated that the dairy farmers and their families comprise two million persons. Their hired help and their dependents number 160,000. Employees in dairy factories and their families come to-
90,000	and employees in fluid milk plants and their families number 120,000. The gross value of the whole dairy industry in Canada in 1953 was estimated at $920 million. '
The cheese producers in my riding particularly have both interviewed me and sent me petitions asking me to protest to the government in the house against the importation of New Zealand cheese. One question the cheese producers would like to know the answer to is whether or not the government intends to permit further imports of New Zealand cheese. The only answer they have received so far was given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in reply to a question asked by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe). As found at page 187 of Hansard of January 14, he said:
Perhaps I could answer that question, Mr. Speaker. We do not expect any further substantial shipments of cheese from any source for at least six months and probably at least nine months.
Why we want cheese imported into Canada in six months or nine months when cheese' production is at its peak I would not know. Neither the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) nor the Minister of Agriculture-(Mr. Gardiner) has as yet given any reasonable explanation to this house as to why New Zealand cheese was permitted to enter Canada, especially so at a time when there is well over 41 million pounds of cheese in storage which is at least 10 million pounds in excess of other years; also at a time when the cheese producers have collected from their own members a very large sum of money in order to finance the export of cheese to the United Kingdom. They have collected a sum of approximately 17 cents a hundred pounds of milk which in the average factory would cost the patron at least $100 to $130 a year.
The cheese producers of Ontario own over ten and a half million pounds of cheese. According to the press they owe the bank on guaranteed loans $3,300,000. To liquidate that cheese today in view of the competition with the cheese from New Zealand they would' probably suffer a great loss. We are told or are led to believe, that the cheddar cheese

The Address-Mr. G. S. White of New Zealand costs approximately 25 cents to 26 cents a pound on the dock at Montreal. There is a tariff of one cent a pound on cheese which amounts to about 4 or 5 per cent. Compare that to industry which has a protection of approximately 20 to 25 per cent.
Other speakers in this debate have pointed out to the government that in years gone by a decline in the purchasing power of the farmer has always led to unemployment. Today we have a decline in the purchasing power of the farmer. This decline in the purchasing power will be further aggravated by the importation of Cheddar cheese from New Zealand. It may be that cheese producers of Ontario are suffering a great and heavy loss if the government permits further importation of cheddar cheese from New Zealand. The importation of this cheese into Canada has been described by one federation official as the worst slap in the face Ontario farmers have ever received.
I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture or his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce what action, if any, the government intends to take in order to prevent further shipment of cheap cheddar cheese from New Zealand.
At page 20 of Hansard of January 10, 1955, in reply to a question, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made this comment:
During the war years a permit was required to import cheese for the reasons stated by my hon. friend, but at the moment cheese is not under price support so far as I am aware.

and the selling agency will arrange to have the cheddar cheese producers pay to the milk producers an equivalent price in terms of fluid milk, less manufacturing costs.
3.	The selling agency will make no payment to the cheddar cheese producers subsequent to the initial payment unless such subsequent payment is first approved by the governor general in council.
4.	The selling agency will market such cheddar cheese to the best advantage possible.
5.	For the purpose of this agreement, processing, carrying and selling costs shall include transportation, storage, shrinkage, handling, colouring, waxing, interest and finance charges, insurance, accounting, selling commissions and other processing and marketing costs, and all other expenditures properly included in an operating account, the total of which shall not exceed two and three-eighths cents per pound; provided that in the case of any unforeseen expenditure in excess of normal processing, carrying and selling costs, the minister may, subject to the approval of the governor general in council, increase the total amount of the costs allowed under this clause.
And now we come to the important clause, where it says:
6.	The minister undertakes that if the average wholesale price of all cheddar cheese produced in the province of Ontario during the year 1954 and marketed by the selling agency according to the terms of this agreement is less than the average initial payment, together with the actual processing, carrying and selling costs which shall not exceed the maximum fixed in clause 5 hereof, there shall be paid to the selling agency the amount, if any, by which the average initial payment together with such costs exceeds the average wholesale price aforesaid.
7.	The books and accounts of the selling agency shall be inspected and audited by an accountant or professional auditor as provided by section 6 of the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, and the report of such accountant shall be submitted to the minister as required.
There are several other clauses which do not apply particularly, but I should like to point out that under clause 6 the minister agrees and undertakes to pay a set price, or to pay a price which would put a floor under cheese. This agreement has been amended by P.C. 1955-30 of January 4, 1955. The amendment is trifling, extending the time to April 30, 1955, and making provision whereby certain further payments will be made over and above the initial price.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has said that cheese is not controlled. He has also said that the legislation does not cover cheese so that it
could be brought under the Export and Import Permits Act. I think the order in council I have read and the agreement made as a result of the order in council show clearly that cheese is an article being supported under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, being one of the acts referred to in section 5 of the Export and Import Permits Act.
So I say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the government has the necessary machinery and the authority to bring cheese under the Export and Import Permits Act, thereby prohibiting or controlling any further imports of cheddar cheese from New Zealand. I think before the debate closes the cheese producers of Ontario would like to have some statement either from the Minister of Trade and Commerce or from the Minister of Agriculture as to whether or not they intend to bring cheese under the Export and Import Permits Act, or whether they intend to permit further shipments of cheap cheddar cheese into Ontario, thus causing loss to the cheese producers of that province.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to be associated wth all members in the House of Commons from Saint John to Victoria who have tfiken part in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As all hon. members are aware, this throne speech gives an indication of the state of the nation; and if it is to give a true picture I believe it is the duty of members to place before the house the state of the nation in its more limited aspects, as it affects their own constituencies. And that is what I shall do in the time allotted to me this afternoon.
It is always in order and a matter of courtesy to extend congratulations to all those deserving of them in the House of Commons, and in that group the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) must be included. There seems to be some hesitancy on the part of some members to extend congratulations to those people who have given service throughout the past year in the forum of government. I am sure however that the government need not feel unduly displeased because of that. So far as Liberal governments are concerned, certainly they are not flattered by praise nor are they dejected by criticism. The people of Canada expect Liberal governments, as a matter of duty, to be patient and progressive and, irrespective of praise or condemnation, Liberal governments in the past have, and I am sure Liberal governments of the future will deliver that service to the very greatest extent of their ability, to all the people of Canada so as to
336	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Studer have this country continue to be what even some socialists admit-the best country on the face of the earth.
As hon. members were told last year, the constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek is one of the greatest in Canada. It is my hope this afternoon, after listening to some of the damp, depressing, death-around-the-corner speeches we have heard during the last week, to present a somewhat more optimistic picture of what is in evidence throughout the country.
It is not my purpose to minimize the difficulties that we face in the country, or the problems, nor is it my purpose to underrate the fact that there are some good things in this country, and I believe that if more emphasis were put on some of the good things of the country than on some of the bad things that may exist we would all maintain a proper balance in regard to the situation in Canada today. When we hear the people who have no hope and who live in despair speak, they talk about unemployment-and there is unemployment. It is an evil that should be eradicated. Yet, there are well over five million people employed in Canada, five million people who are able to earn their own living at perhaps as high wages as earned by any people in the world. That is not done as a matter of course; it did not come about on account of any socialist party or policy in Saskatchewan or anywhere in the world. It came about because of Liberal principles that have been in evidence not only in Canada but throughout the whole world. Those Liberal principles reflect themselves in free trade throughout all of the world, which bring us to a united front and a united attack upon the evils that may exist not only in Canada but throughout the whole world.
Therefore I should like to talk of some of the good things in this country. One of the best things that I know of in this country is food. One of the accomplishments of Liberal policies throughout the years is production which has resulted in plenty. If there are still problems in regard to distribution you will never solve them unless you also have plenty to distribute, or the production that is necessary in order to solve the problem of distribution.
It is a good thing to talk about food; it is something that is a primary necessity of life. Any government in any part of the world that puts emphasis on food, to make sure that food is produced to the ultimate to feed the hungry people of the world, is the type of government that gives the greatest service to all of the people of the world. In my 

constituency, Swift Current-Maple Creek, comprising 300 miles from one corner to the other, there is at the present time an abundance not only of food but of oil and minerals -even dinosaurs are being taken out of the ground, which may or may not mean anything, according to some scientists' interpretation. We have some manufacturing, but the great emphasis is on food in the southwest corner of Saskatchewan, and in Swift Current-Maple Creek. Food is vital; food is a necessity. The question most often asked in the whole world is, when do we eat, and what do we eat?
In my constituency there are 16,500 square miles of land, comprising 10J million acres, practically all of which is under cultivation or used for ranching, and which provides' an abundance of food, if nature is kind to us, which is of value because it creates national wealth that others may distribute throughout the length and breadth of this country. Although we have heard of drought, of dust and of all the evils of the 1930's in that part of the country, no part of the world has recuperated faster than southwestern Saskatchewan has. And this area, above all other areas in western Canada that suffered from drought in the past, is in the best position this year to understand the situation because we have suffered much from years of drought in that part of Canada. We have taken advantage of the policies of the federal government in such matters as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and all the other services provided by the federal government, and we have recuperated in that part of the country on a basis that we hope will be permanent. Therefore, in words that I hope all of us can understand, Mr. Speaker, and that you may like, I should like to present the production of Swift Current-Maple Creek in the form of a menu, a menu which we, the people of Swift Current-Maple Creek as producers, can place on the tables of 250,000 Canadians 365 days a year, produced from that land of over 10 million acres. For breakfast we offer you not a commodity that is manufactured but the ingredients that go into the commodity. For breakfast we offer you porridge made from the finest of oats for the finest people on earth, with milk and cream from the Jersey and Ayrshire and Holstein herds that are second to none. We offer you bacon from the leanest Yorkshires and Tamworths in the whole country. We offer you eggs from the finest flocks of Leghorns, Barred Rocks and New Hampshires in the country that any man would care to see, west of the Ottawa valley. We offer you toast made from the best wheat grown anywhere, and we give you honey that has won

prizes in Toronto and Saskatchewan last year and this year, honey produced by the busiest bees in Canada.
For lunch we offer you, Mr. Speaker, roast leg of lamb and scalloped potatoes, from potatoes that weighed three pounds this year. We offer you rye rolls made from grain and rye grown in the grain and rye fields of my constituency. We offer you butter which is the finest made in creameries throughout the length and breadth of this area. We offer you crabapple jelly made from the Dolgo crab of my constituency, and there is none better in Canada. By the way, I produced 1,200 bushels of apples on my farm this year, and I hope in the future to produce about 3,000 bushels. We also won the trophy in the Saskatchewan fruit show this year.
But that is not all. We now offer you dinner, and first as an aperitif we will offer you rye and water. We have lots of rye in that country. We offer you a choice of sirloin of beef or broad-breasted turkey, such as are grown nowhere else in Canada. We offer you vegetables which are grown with a minimum amount of moisture. Anything grown with a minimum of moisture is of high quality, be it wheat, beef or vegetables. We offer you tomatoes and also macaroni made from Durum wheat grown in my constituency and, as the piece de resistance, Saskatoon berry pie. If you have not eaten it you have not lived. That is what we as producers place on the tables of 250,000 Canadian families 365 days a year. The only reason I mention this is to indicate that the importance of agriculture in this country cannot be overestimated.
Over and above that wheat and beef required by the 250,000 families, we can supply more than a million people in Canada, because my constituency is one of the greatest and best agricultural areas in Canada.
I said I was going to talk of some of the good things in this country, after hearing about all of the bad things. One of the greatest encouragements came to my desk this morning that anyone could ever have. After listening to the socialist speeches in the House of Commons, I found on my desk this morning one of the socialist papers, which is printed in Saskatchewan. It is called the Commonwealth. Here is the headline: "Figures show big growth in Saskatchewan economy." Can you beat that? How can we talk about difficulties in Canada-and we have difficulties-how can the socialists and others talk as they have been when their own paper denies what they have said? Irrespective of that, there are difficulties in agriculture. Agriculture has never been in existence anywhere when it was in the same position as other
The Address-Mr. Studer industries. Everyone knows of the vagaries of nature, the conditions under which we operate, the inability to control prices of any kind. We are subject to every condition that can react against us.
Irrespective of the fact that these figures show a growth in Saskatchewan economy, I am not suggesting that there is not room for improvement in agriculture in Saskatchewan. We have made some advances in agriculture in regard to some stabilized prices, especially in regard to wheat. Let us hold what we have. We should at least support a government that has influence throughout the world with the trading nations of the world. Let us support that government which has the only system that can hold that advance. We have to trade with the people of the world because we cannot create an economy of our own. We cannot continue indefinitely to pay subsidies to one group at the expense of another, because if we do so we will have to take money from one group and pay it to another, thereby diminishing the purchasing power of certain sections of the population. We do not want subsidies. We want to expand the economic wealth of the country and raise the standard of living throughout the dominion and, incidentally, transmit that standard of living to other countries.
There are other important industries in Canada but none of them are as important as agriculture because it means the production of food. You must first eat, and there is nothing else you can do if you do not eat.
In this house we have 23 lonesome farm representatives, 23 who are endeavouring to fight perhaps the greatest battle that any group of men could take on, and they are fighting that battle for the benefit of the agricultural industry without which all the rest of our organizations, our standard of living and our social services must deteriorate.
Therefore, when we hear hon. members in this house talking about cattle, hogs, poultry, and the need for floor prices and parity prices under the agricultural support act, these hon. members are actually speaking on behalf of us all. They are talking about your future because they are advocating policies that will guarantee your future. Once agriculture goes asunder, then all the industries of Canada will fall asunder. Purchasing power will be disrupted. Every member of this house and all the people throughout Canada will be guaranteed food and will continue to eat if hon. members will in turn guarantee the agricultural industry its demands.
This industry has never asked too much, though it has always been in a position where

The Address-Mr. Studer it is deficient. We always hear about legislation in regard to subsidies to farmers. But if farmers ask for that sort of assistance it is because they are short, and it is in order to keep their industry alive and in full production that they ask for these things. We do not ask for anything we do not think is necessary and we do not ask any more than other sectors of industry in Canada.
But we want to guarantee that we are going to continue to have a high standard of living, to which as Canadian citizens we are all entitled, so that we will all be able to meet the trials and tribulations that lie ahead.
We are now wondering how to accomplish this. I do not know of any method of determining what percentage of wealth is accorded to various groups within the economy. But we should determine the labour that enters into agriculture and into every other industry and then as a result of that decide what proportion of the Canadian people in their various groups are getting too much or too little. When there is an injustice that injustice should be corrected.
We have not the talking or voting power of labour. There are 636,000 farmers in Canada and 5,530,000 workers in general industry, and the latter have the strongest bargaining and voting power. It should not only be the farmers who are asking the people of Canada to come to the assistance of the agricultural industry because we are weak and lack the necessary bargaining power.
We are weak in voting power and if we had the strength there would be a different situation in Canada today. No other industry has the paramount need of stabilization that agriculture has. The farmer's share of the national wealth is extremely difficult to determine. It must be remembered that the farmer's family is also working and producing, and that is a fact that is often overlooked. The farmer's wife contributes extensively to farm operations.
I have an article here written quite recently by an Ontario economist who estimated that the services of the farmer's wife were worth approximately $69,000 over a period of 40 years, provided she was normally industrious-and most farmers' wives have to be.
A western economist puts the figure at approximately $173,000. That works out at approximately $4,000 per year. That is not too great a figure when we come to consider what should be the farmer's share of the national wealth.
If commissions are appointed here in Canada, then I think one of the most important tasks to be undertaken by such a body
would be the determination of what share of the national wealth should be accorded to each of our major industries. If we can determine that, then we do not need to listen through thousands of speeches in the House of Commons. We do not have to take things for granted. We do not have to read newspaper articles with regard to the actual conditions which govern the economy of Canada.
When this commission is set up, and I hope it will be soon, we will then be in a position in western Canada to know whether or not we are having a share of the national wealth equal to that offered to other industries in the Dominion of Canada.
Proof of the farmer's position is to be found in the income tax returns. Those returns show that the farmer is sixteenth on the list in regard to receipts. Fishermen are even worse, for they are seventeenth on the list. I will not mention who is at the top of the list or even comes into second place, but something should be done about the farmer's low position on that scale.
As we all know, the farmer's purchases are limited by the amount of revenue he receives, and if we safeguard the farmer's interests, then we will be safeguarding our own.
We have often heard references in this house to a bill of rights. And I think it is high time the farmers of this country had a bill of rights. Last year Senator Humphrey, of St. Paul, Minnesota, proposed a bill of rights, and it may interest hon. members to hear what it contained. It reads as follows:
1.	The right to full equality of economic opportunity.
2.	The right to improved standards of rural living.
3.	The right of reasonable protection against natural hazards.
4.	The right to extend agricultural free enterprise through co-operative action.

speechtext: Tell the Liberal government that.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext: What was that?

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext: Why not get that policy adopted now by the Liberal government?

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
This government was not born with a silver spoon in its mouth, like some members of parliament. I was not born with a silver spoon in my -mouth. I hope I am not boasting, but I had to go out to work at the age of 12 and I have been working ever since, doing a man's work and providing something which is of value to this country. I did not have a socialist, university education handed to me on a platter. I was not born in a log cabin, and I was not born in

The Address-Mr. Studer
a sod shack, but my parents moved into one as soon as they could afford it. The bill of rights continues:
5.	The right to public co-operation and assistance in saving the soil.
6.	The right to preserve the social and human values of family farming.
7.	The right to decent land tenure which would encourage the desirable goal of farm ownership.
Try that in Saskatchewan.
8.	The right (of a farmer) to a democratic voice in his own farm program.
9.	The right to benefits of an expanding world trade.
10.	The right to a long-term program of food storage to encourage abundance.
That is the bill of rights for farmers. That is the sort of program to which we should all subscribe. That is the bill of rights every hon. member should be advocating; for again by protecting the agricultural industry we would be protecting ourselves.
We have agricultural difficulties. We cannot sell wheat. But that wheat will be sold, and I believe that within eight months we will no longer be talking about the problem. We cannot deliver to the elevator of our cnoice. But whatever our difficulties are out in Saskatchewan, they are of a temporary nature and will be corrected.
Production difficulties are permanent difficulties existing in western Canada and particularly in southwestern Saskatchewan, and those are the difficulties we wish to see eliminated. But I would add that we also have had the problem of empty granaries in southwest Saskatchewan, rather than full ones. We also want a floor price, and a good floor price, on eggs. They talk about somebody not receiving the floor price on eggs. All the Saskatchewan government needs to do is to implement their marketing legislation, buy up all the eggs in Saskatchewan and sell them back to the federal government. There is the solution. Will they do it? I do not think that they will. It is much wiser politically not to give consideration to that solution but rather come down here to the House of Commons and tell the federal government what to do.
Then there is the matter of the floor price on hogs. I am glad that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) yesterday took up the problem of the underhog. It is about time he had his day. The only thing I think he recommended was a change in grading. From what I know I think perhaps the hon. member for Selkirk thinks there are not sufficient grades in hogs. But if he would need one more in order to sell his product, I think we should enter another grade of hogs and it would be called the razorback class.
Some of the solutions are right at the socialists' back door. But will they take them? No, they will not, because talk is cheaper.
One of the difficulties in Canada is taxes. We have our provincial taxes. As you know, we have a provincial treasurer in Saskatchewan. His name is Fines; and everybody knows that we are fined for everything in Saskatchewan. We also have our federal taxes. We have the greatest tax, which is for national defence, and who is more responsible for the tax for national defence than are these socialists and their cohorts? Why? Because in the Regina manifesto they stipulate that they will not rest content until this system under which they have lived and prospered shall be eradicated. And the other reason why that national defence expenditure is incurred is on account of their cohorts, wherever they may be in the world. Listen to this:
Thirty-five years ago Lenin made a prophecy that "first we will take eastern Europe; then the masses of Asia; then we will encircle the United States of America, which will be the last bastion of capitalism. We will not have to attack it because it will fall like an over-ripe fruit into our hands ..."
Again, in 1930 Dmitri Z. Manuilsky, who later presided over the United Nations security council in 1949, when addressing the international students at the Lenin school of political warfare in Moscow came out with the somewhat astonishing "war to the hilt between communism and capitalism is inevitable. Today, of course, we are not strong enough to attack. Our time will come in twenty or thirty years. To win we shall need the element of surprise. The bourgeoisie will have to be put to sleep. So we shall begin by launching the most spectacular peace movement on record. There will be electrifying overtures and unheard of concessions. The capitalist countries, stupid and decadent, will rejoice to co-operate in their own destruction. They will leap at another chance to be friends. As soon as their guard is down, we shall smash them with our clenched fist".
That is why you have to have a defence program in Canada. That statement has never been repudiated. The Regina manifesto has never been repudiated. I wish some good honest-to-God socialist would stand up in this House of Commons and repudiate that whole thing. Then we shall be able to conduct ourselves here in this country on a basis of peace with all people of the world.
What is the policy or the idea behind these socialists? You will remember that last year, when we were having the debate on amendment to the Criminal Code, they had an objection. What was their objection? Every one of them was endeavouring to have the penalty for sedition lowered from 15 years to 5 years. We spent almost a week on that matter. Why? If I am a traitor to this country that has given me my living and if

The Address-Mr. Studer I advocate sedition and I am biting the hand that feeds me, why should I get only 5 years? Why should I not be hanged?

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where do they stand? If and when communism knocks at our door, whom are they going to support? Are they going to support this system which they are pledged to eradicate or are they going to support the communistic system to which they give a little bit of lip service once in a while and condemn in a mild manner on occasion? I have never heard an anti-communist speech in this house or in any other house by these socialists since they have been in this House of Commons. I have never heard a good soul-shaking anticommunist speech by them, and you never will as long as they are associated with those with whom they are associated.
We also have federal taxation but we get something for it. Out in Saskatchewan the only thing you receive for your taxes is more taxes. In Canada here we pay taxes. Certainly we pay federal taxes, but we receive something for them. What do we receive? We receive veterans pensions for our taxes. We receive old age assistance for our taxes. We receive family allowances, old age security, national health, disability pensions and blind pensions. We receive the safeguarding of the nation, the administration of the country, the maintaining of floor prices, the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the bonuses and the subsidies, subsidies on farm feed, railway subsidies, trans-Canada highway, housing loans, farm improvement loans, farm loan board, Veterans Land Act, veterans pensions, unemployment insurance and so on and so forth. I should also mention disability pensions.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) the other day made mention of how this disability pension came about. A little girl in Sherbrooke wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) such a pathetic letter that the Prime Minister just had to inaugurate this disability pension. That is the first time I ever heard any socialist admit that they were not responsible for all pensions.
I would suggest to the socialists that they get into harness, get out of this House of Commons and earn some of the production that they wish to distribute among the people of the world. But in Saskatchewan they just live on capitalistic production. They live on capitalistic money that is paid into Saskatchewan. As it appeared in Hansard last year, the amount of money that is spent

in Saskatchewan by the federal government, irrespective of the production of it, is over $139 million. That money the socialists are using in order to promote socialism. If they had to live on socialist policy and had to produce their own wealth in Saskatchewan, every one of them would be in the poor-house. There is no question about it; every one of them would be there. They are living on capitalistic money in the province of Saskatchewan and capitalistic money has been keeping them in existence in Saskatchewan. Once that capitalistic money is withdrawn, then of course their bubble is burst. There is no question about that. But do not expect anything else in Saskatchewan because few of the socialist leaders know the value of a dollar. Any person who has not earned a dollar by the sweat of his brow does not know the value of it. Hence from this non-producing element that is in existence out in Saskatchewan you can continue to expect higher and higher taxes until our farmers are taxed off the land. That is one of the great overheads that the land carries at the present time and that the farmer has to pay, namely the overhead of taxes in the province of Saskatchewan. I want to warn the rest of the people in Canada to look into that picture in Saskatchewan before Quebec or any province adopts socialism.
So they are living off capitalistic money. How did the socialists get that way? I will tell you how they got that way. How did they become socialists? You will remember that back in 1933 a book came out, published by Dale Carnegie, I believe. It said something about trying to win friends and influence people. Every socialist in Saskatchewan read that book and he used it to advantage, so much so that they almost wrote a book of their own, they did not call it "How to Win Friends and Influence People". That was the original title, "How to Win Friends and Influence People". They entitled their manuscript "How to Win Votes and Fleece People". You see the result in evidence every year since they have been here. The best times that Canada ever had were the times when there was the smallest number of socialists in this House of Commons and that was in the period from 1949 to 1953. As long as the people of Canada send socialists to this House of Commons who are pledged to destroy this system, we shall have the customary result. Why do they say that we should follow a capitalistic country, the United States of America, in our contributions to Colombo? Why do they not present to us for comparison a socialistic country? If they are against the capitalist

system one would think they would never refer to it; but all they are interested in is to keep in office and to keep financing on capitalistic money. The day is coming when they will not continue to exist. You have heard of the communistic slogan: "Workers of the world, unite; you have nothing to lose but your chains." The socialists have a slogan too. Their slogan is: "Irresponsible socialists of the world, unite; you have nothing to lose but your brains".
We have heard some speeches in the house in which objection was taken to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) kissing babies. I hope the Prime Minister continues to kiss babies as long as he is Prime Minister and long afterwards because he kissed babies long before he was ever Prime Minister. I like a person at the head of our government who does not have to make an effort to do something that he has not been accustomed to doing all the days of his life. I like people at the head of our government who are family men and not people who ridicule family men. If the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) thinks he can make little men big by making big men little, that has never happened yet in the history of the world and never will.
I come to another friend of ours in the ranks of the socialists, the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson). You will remember that last year a heifer was lost somewhere in the city of Ottawa which was threatening to destroy the whole city and our hero came to the rescue with a rope. It was like David and Goliath. David wound up his sling-shot and hit a bull's-eye. My hon. friend wound up his rope, let fly and missed the heifer. I do not blame him too much because I think there is something wrong with the hon. member's eyesight. I think he is suffering from myopia. During the past summer he was at a provincial C.C.F. convention in Saskatoon and he made a speech to the convention. He is reported in the Leader-Post of July 21, 1954, as having said:
I went to Ottawa expecting to see the benches filled with intelligent faces. I was disappointed.
I would say that the hon. member, sitting in the back row as he does, would not be able to see much further than the front socialist benches directly in front of him, and I think his statement was well founded. In any event he would not have been able to see any further than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because that member was standing up all the time. If my count is correct that member rose to his feet 700 times in the last session. I think the hon. member for Kindersley is suffering from myopia. I know that the hon. member
The Address-Mr. Studer for Winnipeg North Centre is suffering from athlete's foot. You can imagine that as soon as disability pensions were passed both these men would put themselves in a position where they would eventually be recipients of it.
We have also had some speeches by members of the official opposition. I would refer to them as a paper opposition. I do not mean that they are not worth the paper their speeches are written on; I mean that if you read today's papers you will find out what the opposition is going to say tomorrow. That is why I call them a paper opposition. Inasmuch as that is their policy, I suggest that they take ten newspaper editors from across Canada who have been picked at random, put them in the front benches, and they will do a cracking good job. In fact you could pick ten members of the press gallery at random, put them in those front seats and they would do a very good job for the opposition.
But they will not have to do that. Why? Because we Liberals form our own opposition right within our ranks. That is why the opposition's case is hopeless. We form our own opposition within our own ranks. We guide and advise, reject and add, and admonish our government, so that it is the type of government against which the opposition has about as much effect as the waves around the rock of Gibraltar. But they can improve, and we hope that they do and will eventually make some contribution to the people of Canada.
I think my time is about up, much to the regret of the socialists perhaps, but I want to mention one more thing that should be put into effect in Canada. There should be qualifications for members of parliament.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
That would leave me out, I am sure, but that would be expected. You have qualifications for members for school districts and school boards. You have qualifications for municipal administration and for city administration. You have qualifications all the way from the lowest form of government with the exception that when you come to the highest you can be elected a member of parliament as long as you are not in jail. That is one reason why there are so many socialists here. Since the indemnity has been increased, I think there should be qualifications established for members of parliament so that we will eliminate those from our public life who are professional politicians. Let us eliminate those who have no stake in the country except a political stake, and this is my reason. Go back through history and see what happened so far as the advancing or retarding of humanity is concerned.

The Address-Mr. Studer
What stake did Hitler have in Germany except a political stake? What stake did Mussolini have in Italy except a political stake? What stake did Lenin have, what stake did Stalin have, what stake did Karl Marx or Engels have or any of these individuals? What stake did they have in their countries except a political stake? Therefore I suggest that every member of parliament should have certain qualifications. He should have a job, an occupation, farming, or a vocation, and if he does not spend six months of the year at it he should not be permitted to be a member of parliament. Then there would be no more socialists here. After all, the socialists in Saskatchewan are nothing more or less than socialist profiteers, socialist middlemen reaping a profit from the expenditure of dominion government money in the province. We can get along without them just as the socialists say we can get along without other middlemen.
I was going to talk about unemployment but there is not enough time except to say, what do the socialists do when there is unemployment? The only socialist country I know of that deals with it in any way is Russia, and if there are people unemployed there they are either put in the army or sent to Siberia. What is the socialists' solution? I have not heard it. We are pledged to eliminate the cancer of unemployment-and I claim it is a cancer-from society when it occurs. I also think that the workers in industry should be greater sharers in industry. I cannot see that strikes will be eliminated or that we will eliminate the conflict with respect to the sharing of the national wealth unless that is done.
Our government has the responsibilities. It is not assisted by rabble rousers or socialist malcontents. I do not think there is anything like a rabble rouser in Canada. But we do have to strike a balance in government. Living in the world, I say that as an exporting nation we are dependent not on our own policies alone but on the policies of 73 other countries in the world with which we trade. So we wish to strike a balance. I hope I have contributed to that balance in endeavouring to speak not only of the bad things, the things we wish to eliminate in this world, but also of some of the good things that it has been our privilege as Canadian citizens to enjoy. I am in favour of Liberal policies not only in Canada but throughout the whole world and when that comes about you will have one world with the power of production, which is essential, and a solution of the problem of distribution which will guarantee every man on earth his right to live and his fair share of the wealth of the whole world.

So this Liberal government and all other governments having Liberal policies have fed, clothed, housed and provided health and guaranteed freedom to more people than any other system on earth. We wish to extend these benefits to all people on earth. We want to extend the corporal works of mercy. We want to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, take care of the sick. As long as that is the objective of the Liberal government and party, I hope that by word, action and example I can always be found worthy to be considered as one of them.

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
I intend this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, to make some reference to dominion-provincial relations, and particularly the announcement made the day before yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
Before going on to demonstrate, as I believe I can, that the government's policy is one that is a disservice to Canada, I wish to say that I welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that amendments are to be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I have had the privilege over a number of years of adding my voice to those of members on all sides of the house calling upon the government to make a substantial increase in the burnt-out pension or, to be more correct, the war veterans allowance.
We in the C.C.F. support the demand of the Canadian Legion that the war veterans allowance should be increased from the present figure of $50 in the case of a single man and $90 in the case of a married man to $60 for a single man and $120 for a married man. We all agree that allowable income ceilings should be raised from $720 single to $1,200 single, and from $1,200 married to $2,000 married.
Further we in this group see no reason why the veteran should not be given the benefit of an additional $40 a month when he reaches the age of 70 and is eligible for the old age security pension. We believe that it is unfair and unjust for this government to single out the veterans of Canada and discriminate against them by reducing the amount of the war veterans allowance when those veterans become eligible for the old age security pension.
During the war years and immediately following the government held out to the people of Canada the promise of a new social order. The late prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, had proposals which he set before the people of Canada and which he maintained would result in full employment, including greater social security measures and the national health program. He went further and said that the proposals

would include adequate guaranteed prices tor agricultural products. The late prime minister pointed out that farmers in this country had accepted lower prices during the war, and that they should therefore be guaranteed adequate prices after the war. He also said that if his government were returned to power he would undertake the steps necessary to see that all the provinces of Canada had the financial means to discharge their constitutional responsibilities.
Of the principles outlined, the principle that agriculture should have guaranteed prices has been the first casualty. The Liberal government came back to power in Canada in 1935 and has been in power ever since, and the figures put out by the dominion bureau of statistics show that today agriculture is back in the position it was in the late thirties. Figures from the dominion bureau of statistics show that farm cost of production today, based on 1935-1939 equalling 100, is 238-7. But the price level of farm products is only 220-1. In other words the farmers' cost-price relationship, according to the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics, is even worse today than it was in 1935-1939, when we were still in the depths of a depression. If you want to know why there is unemployment in Canada, if you want to know why farmers are having difficulty in meeting their obligations, you can see the answer in the figures I have just quoted.
We had expected as a result of Liberal promises and commitments that agriculture would be guaranteed adequate prices after the war, because of the low prices accepted during the war. Under the policy of the present government not only are the so-called floor prices inadequate, they do not operate at all.
On December 6 last, speaking to the dominion-provincial conference, the Minister of Agriculture made a public confession that his floor price under eggs was not operating. He said the floor price was 38 cents a dozen, and the producer should be entitled to at least 32 cents a dozen. He quoted figures showing that farmers at Edmonton get 30 cents a dozen, at Winnipeg 27 cents a dozen and at London 37 cents a dozen. The government not only has not adequate floor prices for agricultural products, but the floor prices as set are paper floor prices, phony floor prices, and just so much fiction in the words of the Minister of Agriculture himself. At the dominion-provincial conference he admitted that the farmers were not receiving those prices.
Much has been said about the condition of the wheat producers and the wheat industry in this country. The Minister of Trade and
The Address-Mr. Argue Commerce is always very optimistic. He has said time after time that exports in the current crop year were going away up, that sales were improving, and that there would be very little difficulty.
I believe the trend is toward improvement, but not the way the Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out. The latest weekly publication issued by the board of grain commissioners for the period August 1, 1954, to January 5, 1955, shows that during that period we exported 99-6 million bushels, whereas during the same period of last year we exported 99-7 million bushels of wheat. This year to date exports are as low as last year, and last year was not a good year. So far as exports and sales of Canadian wheat are concerned, we can only hope that the trend is toward improvement.
Farm marketings of wheat this year are away down, from 230-9 million bushels a year ago to just 111-7 million bushels during the present period. Do not let anyone tell you that the main reason western farmers are short of cash today is that they have had a crop failure. The truth is that the western farmer has not been able to market even the small quantities of grain he has threshed. When the present crop year ends the majority of farmers will probably have little grain on their farms. The farmer has been able to keep the elevators filled, and the main reason he has no money is that marketings are down, coupled with the additional fact that the price-cost relationship is adverse. We have in Ottawa today a delegation representing the farm unions of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario. This morning they made a well documented submission to the cabinet requesting, among other things, that the farmers be given adequate support prices, that they be given parity prices for wheat sold in Canada, and adequate floor prices for wheat sold on the international market.
Every important wheat producing country in the world today guarantees a support price to its wheat producers; and if one looks over the wheat support prices of the various countries of the world he sees that the Canadian position is bad indeed. It is right at the bottom of the list. The Argentine wheat producer is guaranteed $2.72 a bushel. The Australian wheat producer gets $1.55 a bushel on domestic wheat, plus a cost of production floor on export wheat. The farmer in Spain is guaranteed $2.73 a bushel, in Japan $2.53, in Greece $2.45, in France $2.95, in Belgium $2.49, in Sweden $2.28, in Turkey $2.28 to $3, in the United Kingdom $2.22, in the United States $2.24 and in West Germany $2.72 to

The Address-Mr. Argue $2.83 a bushel. Canada has the lowest guaranteed price of all, only $1.40 a bushel at Fort William, which means an effective price to the farmer of about $1.20 for No. 2 northern wheat at his local elevator marketing point.
There are three facts about the Canadian wheat picture we should not forget. The first is that the Canadian wheat grower produces the best wheat in the world, but under a Liberal government he is condemned to the highest cost of living in the world and the lowest guaranteed price in the free world. I say that the attitude of the Canadian government as expressed in its treatment of the wheat producers is shameful. No wonder the farmers of western Canada, through their farm unions and other organizations, are considering once again a mass movement on Ottawa to try to impress upon this anti-farm government the need to increase the support price on Canadian wheat.
It is a shame that Canada, one of the wealthiest if not the wealthiest country per capita in the world, should pay its wheat producers the lowest guaranteed price. The agricultural policy of this government is definitely and decidedly against the interests of the producers, and does not in any way give the farmers the guaranteed floor price they were promised by the late prime minister, Mackenzie King, at a time when agriculture was taking such low prices during the period of the war.
We in the C.C.F. believe that the principles laid down in the original dominion-provincial conference following the war were good. We believe that Canadians in every province of Canada are entitled to a basic minimum standard of services. We believe that dominion-provincial agreements are necessary if the government is going to adopt the financial policies necessary in order to maintain full employment. We believe such agreements would be of assistance in connection with the other things proposed to the original conference. We are sorry now that this government is set against implementing those important financial and social security measures. The late prime minister, Mackenzie King, said that just as soon as a sufficient number of provinces signed the taxation agreement he would implement the various social security and full employment measures proposed.
But with the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the policy was changed. Hon. D. C. Abbott, who was minister of finance in December of 1950, said then that even though all the provinces were to sign a taxation agreement the federal government was not committed to anything in any other field.

The government today has demonstrated by its actions that it will not undertake the measures necessary to provide full employment. When the then minister of finance made his budget speech in the House of Commons in the 1954 session he forecast that the real wealth production of Canada would not go up in the coming year. The real wealth production of this country, because of the increasing population and the improvements in technology, should go up by at least 5 per cent every year. Instead of going up by 5 per cent it is forecast that the gross national product is likely to go down to the extent of some $500 million. Even allowing for a poor crop in western Canada, the fact remains that because we did not have full employment in Canada we lost during 1954 approximately $1,200 million in wealth production. That $1,200 million represents sufficient wealth to provide a health insurance program, to increase family allowances and to provide stabilized prices for agricultural products. But the government has allowed production to go down and the people of Canada to lose $1,200 million worth of wealth production.
The day before yesterday the Prime Minister announced unilaterally some of the results of the taxation negotiations he has had with the premier of Quebec. Ordinarily one expects that when two governments Have been making negotiations, any tabling of documents or statements made will be made concurrently. But the federal government made its announcement one day; and the premier of Quebec did not bother making one at all, and did not table the letters until the following day.
I may have some criticisms to make of the premier of Quebec, but certainly I will not malign him to the extent the Prime Minister did, according to a report in the Montreal Gazette, when he made the statement that Canada's prosperity and growth pleased everyone except countries behind the iron curtain and some people in Quebec. I may criticize the premier of Quebec, but I shall never criticize him in those terms; because even though I disagree violently with the stand taken by the premier of Quebec, I say those terms should not be used in relation to a premier of any province in Canada elected by democratic vote.

The statement by the Prime Minister of Canada in which he said that the Canadian income tax law would be amended to reduce the federal tax by 10 per cent in Quebec means, in my opinion, a complete surrender by the federal government of Canada to Premier Duplessis in Quebec.
We were told by the Prime Minister that the 10 per cent reduction represents just about the same amount of money that will be collected by the 15 per cent tax in the way it is applied in the province of Quebec. Now Canada has to go back to the kind of taxation situation, that existed before the war, when taxes varied from one province to another. We have all the ill effects, double taxation and differing taxation, and I am extremely disappointed that the federal government of Canada has yielded to the premier of Quebec in this way. It is a disservice to Canada.

speechtext:
As a nation we are going to suffer from this policy, because it demonstrates that the government has forgotten about the principles enunciated in the dominion-provincial conference following the war. It shows conclusively that this government is not prepared to take those fiscal, taxation and economic measures that are necessary to guarantee full employment and full prosperity.
The result of this reversal of policy and attitude is shown in the fact that in 1954 Canadians lost $1,200 million of wealth production that should have been obtained. It shows that this government has now abandoned the idea of a social security program that would include health insurance. I believe the health insurance proposal, in the original conferences, was one of the most important proposals. The announcement of the Prime Minister demonstrates that he is now surrendering even his plan of a health insurance program.
The proposals in the original dominion-provincial conferences would have made it possible for Canadians living in all provinces of Canada to have a minimum basic standard of provincial services. The provinces have not the taxation resources necessary to fulfil their duties under the Canadian constitution. The revenues of the federal government amount to $4,500 million a year. The revenues of all ten provinces in Canada combined amount to only some $1,400 million a year, and the combined revenues of all the municipal governments in Canada, both rural
The Address-Mr. Argue and urban, amount to some $900 million a year. Therefore, out of the revenue dollar the federal government takes 73 cents, the provinces have 17 cents and all municipal governments have is 10 cents. There is the reason the federal government needs to provide increased grants and measures to enable the provinces to meet their very important obligations under the constitution.
One of their most important obligations is the provision of educational services; another of their most important obligations is the provision of roads which is a vital service in this nation today. The United States government recognized the necessity for an adequate road program as far back as 1912 and provided grants to the states for the building of roads. Today the United States has a good road system and President Eisenhower has proposed that congress provide $101 billion for roads in the United States in the next ten years. If the federal government of Canada did the same thing on a per capita basis it would provide $909 million a year toward the building of roads.
The only item in the estimates provides the magnificent sum of $15 million for the trans-Canada highway. The amount should be $909 million a year if the Canadian government was to make the same contribution to roads on a per capita basis. But ours is a much larger country than is the United States. If the Canadian government were to undertake a road program that would give us the same type of roads, no doubt it would cost a great deal more. Our government should give serious consideration to providing immediately adequate grants for the building of roads in various parts of the dominion.
The United States grants are not just for super highways or even just for ordinary highways in the states, but are for assistance in building every single mile of road in the United States of any consequence whatsoever, even farm to market roads and roads for local school buses. Rural municipalities in Canada, even urban municipalities, where a highway goes through a city, find the provision of adequate roads an impossibility.
The reason municipalities are unable to provide adequate roads in Canada is that the tax base in a municipality is so narrow. Municipalities derive almost all of their revenue from taxation on real property, and the taxation on land and urban properties for roads and for education is becoming almost unbearable in every single province of Canada. If there is an important political issue that is the same in each and every one of the provinces it is this matter of inadequate

The Address-Mr. Argue roads, high land taxation and the inability of municipalities to provide roads on their meagre taxation base.
The same thing is true with respect to adequate educational services. Any country in the world that prides itself on being a democracy and being progressive should provide adequate moneys to create equal educational opportunites for all the young people of that nation. We know the attitude of the premier of Quebec toward university grants. He will not take them. When the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) advocates that the federal government make grants for the provision of equal opportunities for education on the public and high school level, this government allows the attitude of the premier of Quebec to influence it to the point that it says no, we will not make grants for education in Canada. The result is a lowered standard of education in many provinces.
I come back to the statement I made earlier, that the Prime Minister had surrendered-yes almost unconditionally-to Premier Duplessis, as was clearly demonstrated in the statement he made in the house the day before yesterday. He has not only surrendered on the matter of taxation agreements, but he has surrendered to the leader of nationalist ideas, Premier Duplessis, to the point that he says, "No educational grants. We will let the children of Canada suffer from unequal educational opportunity." This attitude is a shame.
I would like to see the federal government, in the dominion-provincial conferences that are coming up, return to its original principles which were presented to the dominion-provincial conference after the war, and even at this late date undertake measures that will provide full employment, and an adequate social security system; and that will mean health insurance now. I hope they will adopt measures that will provide adequate guaranteed floor prices and a fair share of the national income for agriculture, and which will grant to each and every provincial government in Canada the financial resources to carry out its responsibilities under the Canadian constitution.
I do not think the attitude of the premier of Quebec should be allowed to condemn 15 million Canadians to suffer such things as high hospital bills, and high doctors' bills; to cause 15 million Canadians to go without adequate roads and adequate educational opportunities, and the Canadian nation to lose $1,200 million of wealth production in one year.
Again I make the statement that the Canadian government should stop sacrificing the well-being of 15 million Canadians on the

altar of ultranationalism; and, if that statement be considered too strong, I suggest hon. members read the Prime Minister's statement to the Reform club in Quebec last September.
