speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to get to my feet so early in this session because I am sure the general rule about being seen and not heard is as applicable to new members of this house as it is to small children. But times have changed. I know that my two daughters have a great deal more to say than their parents had, so perhaps I may be permitted some slight deviation from the golden rule of silence.	.
I must admit I have been perplexed as to just what opening remarks I might make. I have no desire to make an evangelical speech of condemnation and denunciation. Neither have I any desire to offer wholesale congratulations to the government. Let us face it. As a member of the opposition, that group without which no government can operate efficiently, it is my duty to point out what I consider the shortcomings and deficiencies of this government, and I am prepared to say that this privilege only exists if such criticism can be constructive and a sound alternative offered.
Criticism, of course, either constructive or otherwise, can fall on deaf ears. My leader has conferred upon this government a diploma characterizing them as the greatest free traders of all time. I would confer upon them a degree "in mutual admiration". Perhaps they cannot be blamed for the fact that such a degree can be conferred upon them, because 20 years in office has convinced them that there is no alternative to their type of government.
I believe there is an alternative, and to express my views I might even have to use such unmentionable terms as tariffs, protection, and free enterprise.
What are the problems that face us today? Certainly by far the most important is unemployment. I agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that there is no magic formula which can put an end to unemployment. But if unemployment were as regional and seasonal as the speech from the throne suggests, then I believe the magic formula of government handouts would do the trick. I am sure the Minister of Labour knows as well as we do that the situation now confronting us is much more serious than that. I know that in West York unemployment is greater today than it has been since the depression, and I do not need the benefit of information from the dominion bureau of statistics to convince me of that fact.

But now that we have criticized, have we anything to offer by way of solution? First of all, conditions can only be improved if all three partners in the free enterprise system join in a common program. But who are they? First, labour; second, management or industry; and third, the government. Each has a vital role to play.
To the workingman I would say that we cannot compete for the world's markets without getting more for our production dollar. Let me make it quite clear that I do not believe wages are too high. Far from it. But if businessmen are asked to devise better and more efficient methods of production, to reduce production costs, then I think labour too must join in the same program to see that greater productivity results from each man's daily job.
To management I would say that on you must fall the major burden of achieving the highest production at the lowest cost. Production methods must be constantly under study. The introduction of "automation" in plant equipment, it appears, must more and more be emphasized. New sales techniques must be tried and new markets sought to free us from dependence upon the United States.
Industry has achieved a great deal, but there appears to be an ever-increasing tendency to ask for government assistance even on small matters. Leaders of business must realize that if the government is asked for assistance there can be no satisfactory answer if the government asks for control. And this government shows no reluctance in accepting the principle of controlling every phase of economic life in this country if it is given the opportunity.
I might bring this thought to the special attention of bank presidents, whose lengthy reports I read annually. If the country's credit requirements cannot be met without government guarantees, then tighter and tighter government administrative control can be the only result, ending ultimately in government control of every phase of banking.
What could the government do to relieve unemployment other than the pump-priming job it is doing? I believe it could do a great deal, but this government has done nothing. We do not recommend high tariffs and protection, but we do ask for an end to the naive program of binding us under trade agreements to nations which are not playing under the same rules. The problem is just as simple as that. We choose up sides and we are ready to kick off, when we are informed that our opponent has just built a brick wall on the 20-yard line. With that system the best we can ever do is kick single
The Address-Mr. J. B. Hamilton points. The touchdowns will always be against us; and is that not just what our government has allowed to happen? Our two biggest customers, the United States and Britain, have allowed our goods entry or refused entry as they saw fit, regardless of the GATT agreement.
I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that if industry is called upon to cut down costs, to improve production techniques, and to economize, then I think it has the right to say to this government: "You economize, improve your methods and reduce your taxation program in the same proportion that you have asked us to reduce our prices to get into the world markets." Surely it is not too much to ask this government to reduce its over-all expenditure in the same proportion that has been achieved in the United States in the last couple of years.
This government could help further if it took another look at what I consider to be a very artificial exchange rate on the Canadian dollar. It is readily apparent that the rate is not based on the world's desire for Canadian dollars for trading purposes, because our adverse position in that respect has already been pointed out very forcibly by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). The real demand for Canadian dollars in the world's money market is for capital investment, and the artificially high value placed on the dollar is a real handicap to our manufacturers in their trading position. We should face this issue now because, if we do not, I shudder to think of the situation looming up and what will happen when our foreign investors complete their programs of construction and start asking for their dividends.
Is this not the way this government must face up to the country's unemployment problem? There appears to be no alternative. What will it be? Will it be a continuation of pump-priming, a little loosening up of the purse strings on the workers' and employers' own hard-earned unemployment insurance dollars, or a cold, hard, practical approach to this greatest problem in Canada today?
I think, Mr. Speaker, the spectre of unemployment is a far greater worry to the home owner than to any other individual in the community. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) has emphasized that fact in this house, and has suggested a method of protection for home owners who are buying under N.H.A. I wholeheartedly support the idea of equity of redemption insurance and, as a matter of fact, I strongly advocated such a plan during our recent by-election campaign in West York.

The Address-Mr. J. B. Hamilton
But the real problem lacing the home owner is in his capacity as a shareholder in his municipality. That municipality is having m6re and more trouble meeting its obligations because of its unfortunate position in the tax source picture. I am firmly convinced that we are saddling the municipality with responsibilities far beyond its capacity. I find it very difficult to understand why real estate should be carrying almost the complete load for educational cost, police protection and other similar responsibilities. Surely these items are for the benefit of all persons, not just for the benefit of home owners. I am hoping that when the dominion-provincial conference becomes a fact, the problems of the municipality will receive serious and thorough consideration, because otherwise it is questionable if essential services can be maintained and expanded.
The Minister of Finance should remember that the home owner is entitled to a tax break. His investment in a home is the largest investment of his life. It is an investment in the development of this country. It has created jobs on a greater scale than any investment in common stock in a corporation. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this government has given a tax credit of 20 per cent on dividends received from common stocks to anyone who invests in the same. I say to the Minister of Finance that it is much more important that such a tax credit should be allowed on annual payments of principal on house purchases, and on realty taxes paid on the same.
For example, a purchaser pays $400 in principal on his house mortgage annually, and $200 in realty taxes. Each of these amounts has created employment. It is a real investment, just the same as or more so than an investment in the common stock of one of our corporations. He should receive a credit on his income tax of 20 per cent of the total amount of both principal and realty taxes paid, namely $120. If that formula is not acceptable to this government the least which should be done for the home owner is to allow the real property taxes which he pays on his home as a deduction from his total income for income tax calculation.
I cannot close without mentioning that my constituency of West York has suffered as the result of two major disasters in this country during the past year. First, as the result of the Moose Jaw T.C.A. air crash, it lost its esteemed and highly honoured member of this house, Rodney Adamson, and his wife, Cynthia. I know this house and our party deeply feel his departure from this chamber, as he was a fine parliamentary


representative.	Then late in the year
West York bore the brunt of "Hurricane Hazel". Loss of life and property were appalling, but our people went to work with grim determination. Their efforts and their financial contributions to the various charitable drives have been tremendous.
This sacrifice must not be in vain. Surely this disaster has brought home to this house the necessity for an adequate national civil defence set-up. This program needs more than air raid sirens. It needs an adequate permanent force, small though it may be, just as much as an army does. Let us see that we get it, because I saw municipal authorities working under appalling conditions which should not occur in a well organized society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I have the privilege of rising in the house and speaking on behalf of one of the finest constituencies in Canada. May I first of all join with other members in congratulating the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The way these two hon. gentlemen acquitted themselves was certainly a credit to themselves and to the communities they represent, and was in the finest traditions of the house.
When I say I have the privilege of representing one of the finest areas in Canada I of course am referring to the people of the constituency. There is probably no other rural constituency in Canada whose population is as cosmopolitan as that of Vegreville. It is indeed true that the strength of Canada lies in her diversity. When we take Canada as a whole we find people of different backgrounds, different origins, different traditions, each of whom has something to contribute to the building of a new national Canadian culture and the strengthening of this land. So I say the constituency of Vegreville is most cosmopolitan, and I think you will find there the finest example of unity because the people, regardless of their origin, are able to understand and get along with each other. I also feel, and this is an actual fact, that our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will go down in history as the greatest promoter of unity in Canada.

I listened with a great deal of interest during the course of the debate to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), and especially what he said with regard to tariffs. I wish to assure the house that the people of the province from which I come will endorse his views in this regard. Canada is the third largest trading nation in the world, being exceeded only by the United States and the United Kingdom. The well-being of this nation depends upon the volume of our trade with other countries.
This is true, of course, for every section of our population. It is certainly true of western Canada, for it is essential that the people of the prairies have a market for their wheat and other agricultural products. The same is true of the fisherman, whether he be on the east coast or on the west, and the same is also true with respect to any of the workers in our factories. The fact remains that if we want other countries to buy from us the things that we have to sell, then naturally these other countries will expect that we will buy from them. For that reason high tariffs do not promote trade. Tariffs are always a barrier to trade.
In view of certain restrictions that have been imposed on our exports by the United States government, I realize that some measure of protection is necessary for our industries. It is necessary that we promote their expansion and development and provide more opportunity for the creation of jobs for our people. But I believe the United States is at the crossroads today so far as giving economic leadership is concerned. They will have to decide, and decide soon, whether there is to be more and freer trade among nations. In this respect Canada has had the courage and determination to give leadership in attempting to break down the barriers to such free trade.
As one who represents a farming area, I sometimes find it difficult to tolerate the views held by some individuals who have a fatalistic attitude and regard farming as though it were the worst type of occupation. On the contrary, farming is one of the finest occupations in which one can engage. It may be that I hold this view because I was born and raised on a farm, but the outlook of the farmer is most independent, and with the advent of modern machinery farming no longer is the drudgery that it used to be years ago. I think hon. members will agree with me that with good and careful management most people who go into farming are able to do well.
But farming is also a very risky occupation, and it is often very discouraging and difficult. The farmer is subjected to declines
The Address-Mr. Decore in prices, as was the experience in the hungry thirties. He is subjected to weather conditions such as hail, drought, early frost, bad harvesting weather and, as was the case last year, excessive moisture. We are all aware of the serious crop failure experienced in the three prairie provinces in 1954, especially in the central and northern parts, and we can hardly expect to have another crop failure without disastrous results.
Some reference was made during the course of the debate to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I believe that act, which came into existence in 1939, is a great thing and a wonderful idea, but I agree again with the hon. member for Rosthern that in view of present conditions the payments should be broadened. I might go a step further. I pointed out a moment ago that another crop failure in the three prairie provinces would be disastrous to the farmers, and I wonder whether the government would not give consideration to seeing whether the farmers would not agree to an increase in the contribution they make. At the present time it is 1 per cent. It could very well be raised to 3 per cent or even more.
Perhaps some arrangement could be entered into with the provinces whereby, through the co-operation of the governments of the provinces and the federal government the farmer, in the event of a crop failure, would obtain much greater assistance than he is able to get at the present time. I would be glad if the leaders of the farm organizations would give this matter serious thought. Incidentally, I regard the farm organizations as most desirable and necessary, because their leaders have the opportunity to study various problems, to make suggestions and to advise governments, provincial or federal. For that reason I should like to know the feeling of the farm organizations about the suggestion I have made with respect to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
What I really want to bring to the attention of the house and the government is another problem which I consider to be serious, and which we are being confronted with in the farming communities. I am of course referring to the great difficulty that young men and women must overcome if they want to start farming. We realize that it requires a lot of capital, and because of lack of capital it is difficult for these young men or other people who are interested to make a start. We all realize that the very high cost of machinery as well as the very high cost of land probably requires a minimum investment, in 'our area at least, of $15,000 to start a farm. There are many people who wish to make a start who just do not have that kind of money.

The Address-Mr. Decore
When my grandfather came to this country some 60 years ago he was able to obtain a homestead upon the payment of a $10 fee. We are now living in a different age, however, and under different conditions. I think we still have enough of the pioneering spirit left in us, but as I say it still requires a lot of capital. You will find instances of families where there are four or five boys, and these families are able only to set one boy up farming. The other lads just are not able to make a start. They must move into some industrial centre such as Hamilton or Toronto in order to find a job.
What about the farm hands who are employed on salary? It is most difficult for them to save enough money to be able to make a start in farming. The same thing applies to many of our newcomers. Why should many of these people who have the qualifications and the desire find it necessary to move into industrial centres? There was a time when industrial centres were able to absorb these people, but often they only add to the problem of unemployment.
If I may digress for a moment, one of the serious problems we have in the prairie provinces is the lack of a self-sustaining population. If you were to compare the 1941 census with the census of 1951, which is the last census, you would find that in Alberta, although there was an apparent gain of some
140,000	people during that period, actually it was not a true picture of the situation because that figure does not take into account a very important factor, namely the natural increase. When I speak of the natural increase I am referring to the number of births in excess of the number of deaths. We have very accurate figures in that respect. When you take these figures into account you will find that the net loss of population in Alberta for that ten-year period was 9,500.
That is not very serious, but if you take the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan the figures are much more serious and disastrous. In Manitoba the net loss of population was over 65,000. In the province of Saskatchewan there was a net loss of over 200,000. Therefore, you will readily see that the net loss of population in the three prairie provinces during that period from 1941 to 1951 was over a quarter of a million. This shows that we not only have failed in that period to attract people, but have failed to even keep those people who were already there. Many of these people have moved into industrial centres because they are areas where there is a great population^ and a greater population offers better opportunities.
My point is that, whether in the prairie provinces or in any other province of Canada

it is our young men and women who wish to go into farming and who have the necessary experience and desire who should be given an opportunity to remain on the land. I believe they would be able to make a much more valuable contribution to the wealth of this country if they were encouraged to remain on the farms where they desire to be. The fact is that it is almost impossible for a man to make a start in farming because of the amount of capital that must be involved.
What can be done about it? I can only offer a suggestion. May I point out that at one time it was impossible for many Canadians to own their own homes, and then along came the national housing plan. That plan was by no means perfect. It still probably needs changes. Some changes have already been proposed by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). But the fact is through the operation of this act thousands of people in towns and cities became home owners who otherwise never would have been able to own a home.
What actually happened was that a scheme or a plan was set into motion without any risk on the part of the government or on the part of the lending institutions. It is not a case of a handout. It is a plan which was put into motion and which has brought a benefit to thousands and thousands of people in this country. I therefore ask why there should not be a similar plan for our young men and women who wish to go into farming.
I am not suggesting handouts. Some of you will say we already have legislation which tends to assist the farmers, such as that setting up the Canadian farm loan board or the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This legislation is intended to assist those people who have already made a start in farming. It is a case of enabling them to buy better equipment, improve their homes, or purchase additional land. But as far as I know there is nothing on our statute books which would tend to help the people who wish to make a start on the farm, along the lines of the national housing scheme.
Mr. Speaker, a plan similar to the National Housing Act, possibly with the co-operation of the provincial governments, could be, I think, brought into existence. Let me point out that we have already the basic machinery to set up this kind of a plan. We have the V.L.A. offices in various provinces. They already have the know-how, the knowledge to deal with these matters.
Since there is great room for expansion of our agricultural industry in this country I do not think we want these people who are suited for farming and who have a wide background of experience in that occupation to go into

something else when they are desirous of going into farming. I do hope the government will give this matter very careful consideration.

It is
not my intention today, Mr. Speaker, to contribute unnecessarily to the prolongation of this debate. However, there are a number of matters of vital concern to the residents of Fraser Valley, which electoral district it is my honour to represent. Therefore I shall endeavour to present them and deal with them as briefly as possible, while stressing them as vigorously as I believe their importance and urgency would warrant. As you are no doubt aware, the economy of the Fraser valley is quite diversified, and the problems to which I shall refer today have to do with different aspects of our economy.
A great part is played in my riding by those who are engaged in the fishing industry, and during the past several weeks it has been my privilege to discuss with them some of the problems with which they are currently faced. I should like first of all to refer to the closure regulations which are affecting them at the present time. I believe that as these regulations are imposed they will bring additional hardship on our people in this industry.
Last year the department announced that the closure on commercial fishing in the Fraser river above New Westminster bridge would be in effect on September 16, as a conservation measure. Following strong protests this decision was altered and the closure date for 1954 was set at October 8, for 1955 at September 30 and for 1956 at September 15. This modification was welcomed by the fishermen in this area, and in a letter to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) I expressed the hope that after further consideration and investigation it might not be necessary to apply the earlier closures as set out in the statement.
Regarding the effectiveness of the closure measures last fall, I should like to read a short paragraph from the brief submitted by the gill net section of the Pacific fishermen and allied trades union. It states with respect to closure:
At the time the suggestion contained in article 5 appeared our organization sent a brief to the federal minister of fisheries and also told him at an interview in Vancouver that the proposed measure would not only work a very great hardship on the fishermen and the businessmen of the area, but that the measure would not have the desired effect, i.e., to increase the number of parent fish reaching the local streams between New Westminster and Mission. There being no pink salmon run to the Fraser this year, commercial fishing was allowed to October 8 and then closed supposedly to conserve the chum salmon. Our contention was fully borne out by the fact that up to December 1,
The Address-Mr. Patterson
(when all commercial fishing automatically closed by custom in past years in the Fraser river) the showing of chums in the local streams mentioned was the poorest in history, showing plainly that the stopping of fishing above New Westminster bridge had no bearing on the matter.
Therefore I suggest that further consideration be given to this matter. As I have already said, I hope that in the future earlier closures such as have been suggested will not be imposed.
There was also the suggestion that the closure would prevent the taking of a poor grade of fish, which would obtain above this specified point in the river. In this connection I would call attention to two letters, one of which is written by the secretary of this union to the Johnston Fishing and Packing Company of New Westminster, British Columbia. It states:
Gentlemen, the directors of the gill net section of our union are desirous of obtaining information as to the procedure used in handling salmon caught above New Westminster bridge. As you probably know, there have been a lot of loose statements as to the quality of salmon caught in this area and in order to arrive at the facts of the case we would be very much obliged if your company could answer the questions listed below.
1.	In deliveries of salmon from your collectors to your plant are the salmon caught and collected above New Westminster bridge kept entirely separate at all times from salmon caught and collected in other parts of district 1?
2.	In the process of canning salmon at your plant is a separate code mark used to differentiate between salmon caught above New Westminster bridge and salmon caught in other parts of district 1?
3.	Does the government laboratory require certification from your company as to the place or origin of any parcel of canned salmon submitted by your company for inspection?
4.	What percentage of this year's total pack was of grade "b" quality which was canned at your plant?
Thanking you in advance for this and other information which may occur to you as pertinent to the quality of salmon caught above New Westminster bridge, I am,
Yours sincerely,

Pacific Fishermen and Allied Trades Union,
298 Main St.,
Vancouver 4, B.C.
Attention Mr. Fred Rolley,
Dear Sir:
Replying to yours of the 4th instant in which you ask four questions dealing with the Fraser river fishing operations, our answer to the first three is "No" and to the fourth "None".
Therefore we have a picture of the situation as it exists, relative to the suggestion and contention that above the New Westminster bridge the fish are of poorer quality.
Another matter of concern to the fishermen is that while the maximum length of gill

The Address-Mr. Patterson nets for use in the Fraser river is only 150 fathoms, that allowed in the past in other areas, and for seiners, is 200 fathoms. Fishermen have told me that 150 fathom nets are only about 50 per cent effective, as the nets have a tendency to gather, whereas on the other hand 200 fathom nets remain at approximately their full length. In this respect these men are wondering why gill nets are all to be reduced to 150 fathoms while no reduction is contemplated for the seiners. There is also dissatisfaction over the fact that while gill netters are under constant and close inspection, little if anything is being done to enforce the regulations with respect to the seiners.
Then I have one further observation to make about the fishing industry. Last year a statement was made to the effect that a number of reconstructed seiners were to be permitted into Canada and given some tax concessions. They were required to spend at least two years in the deep-sea fishing industry. It is now brought to my attention that last fall at least one of these vessels was reported fishing right up to the very mouth of the river. The gill netters of the Fraser river are concerned about this and other problems to which I have referred, and are of the opinion that a concerted effort is being made, by restrictive measures imposed against small and independent fishermen, to force them out of the industry, so that further benefits will accrue to the large company-owned seine boats.
I call these matters to the attention of the minister and suggest that he will have to do a lot of fast talking-perhaps faster than usual-to convince fishermen that this is not so, if indeed it is not.
The second problem to which I would call attention is that of river bank erosion and flood danger. It appears that at least some of these problems are characteristic of the Fraser valley. I have not heard other members dwell upon	them	at	length in	anyrespect, but	I can	say	that they	affectmightily the	Fraser	valley. Before	coming to Ottawa for	this	session I	spent
a good portion of one afternoon in the company of the reeve of Kent municipality, inspecting the river and protection work at several locations. There certainly is cause for immediate concern. From the annual report of J. L. MacDonald, provincial diking commissioner, contained in the report of the land service for the year ended December 31, 1953, and reported in the Fraser Valley Record, I quote the following:
Within the memory of many the Fraser river has washed away vast acres of fertile land, replacing homes and farms with gravel bars. This destructive action is continuous. The effects are especially

evident in the districts of Kent. Nicomen island, Matsqui and Pitt Meadows. On Nicomen island the Department of Public Works has had to move a road located outside the dike back from the river bank three times within a year. Remedial action will have to be taken.
To find a solution to the problems which should attempt to control the cause, is not a simple matter. It will require comprehensive engineering investigation and study.
Corrective measures are beyond the scope of local districts. The subject is of importance both to British Columbia and Canada.
In the one district of Kent I understand 1,200 acres of valuable agricultural land have been lost. At the present time farms are in immediate danger as the process of erosion continues. At one point the river threatens to break through the bank completely and cut another channel. If this were to happen, not only would it be disastrous to the farmers but it is questionable whether navigation would be possible through that section at low water.
Engineers have made a survey of the area and estimate that the cost of the required work would be in the neighbourhood of $43,500. The municipality is committed to $7,000 for river bank work during the current year, and it is completely beyond the ability of the district to assume further responsibilities at the present time. The nature of the problem is such that further delay in its solution will be disastrous not only to the few farmers near the bank but also to the entire community.
I might say in this connection that the natural process of erosion is tremendously aggravated by the passage of tug boats. These boats keep close to the bank in order to miss the strong currents, and one can stand and watch the wash as it strikes the bank and then recedes, carrying soil with it. We do appreciate the assistance given by the dominion government in this matter, but we urge that an effort be made to solve the whole problem permanently and allay the fears of those people who are in danger of losing large parts of their farms. What is true in Kent is likewise true in the other areas I have already mentioned, and also in Albion, further down the river.
I should like to refer again, as I did last year, to a matter which concerns the residents of another section of the Fraser valley, namely those who are living along the Vedder river. This matter has been brought to the attention of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources by the officials of the department of agriculture of the British Columbia government. The whole proposition has been presented, with aerial photographs and all the data required, and we were hoping that some positive action would be taken in this respect. We had

hoped that the dominion government would be prepared to give some substantial assistance in this matter. The Vedder river is gradually filling up the channel, until at the present time we find that for possibly three miles there is very little channel, and the river just meanders here and there. It is quite possible, in the event of a flash flood, that the whole area would be under water.
There are some valuable dominion government works in that section. Even although it is the judgment of certain officials that they are not in danger at the moment, there is a definite possibility that they would be in danger in the event of a serious flood developing. Therefore I again request that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources further consider this matter and render some assistance in its solution.
Once again it appears that the government does not intend to do anything toward raising the pensions of our senior citizens. I have listened to the speeches of hon. members from day to day, and the fact that very few have even referred to this matter has given me some cause for surprise. I believe the senior citizens of our country are deserving of some real consideration at the present time. It appears that many of those citizens who have worn themselves out in building up our great country are to be forced to spend their remaining days in actual want, and that certainly most of them are in far from comfortable circumstances. The governments of British Columbia and Alberta have recognized the need for some action and are now supplementing the old age security payment by $15 a month. I understand that Saskatchewan still holds to the $2.50, and the other provinces are not contributing anything in this regard.
Last year this government balked at raising the war veterans allowance because they said it would jeopardize the progress of their social welfare program, but we find this year they have introduced legislation to raise the war veterans allowance. I do not know how much the increase will be, but I certainly hope it will be substantial. We hope that if this government cannot find it possible to increase old age pensions at this session- we hope they do-they will be prepared next session to bring in legislation to give better consideration to those who are elderly, to enable them to meet their living costs.
I have the honour to represent one of the great agricultural areas in British Columbia. One of the main problems confronting those engaged in certain aspects of agriculture in that area is the high prices they are forced to pay for feed grains. I have no quarrel with the prairie farmers in their endeavour 50433-23
The Address-Mr. Patterson to obtain a greater share of the national income. I believe it is coming to them; but the farmers in my area do object to paying a terrifically high price for products for which the farmer receives very little.
For instance, I have been given to understand that the farmer receives approximately $28 a ton for feed wheat. When our poultry raisers in British Columbia purchase feed wheat it costs $68 to $70 per ton. The freight charge from Regina to Vancouver would be in the neighbourhood of $13.40 per ton. Someone somewhere is receiving 100 per cent profit. I believe this situation warrants investigation, for this problem is of vital concern to the farmers in the Fraser valley and is one to which I sincerely direct the attention of the government at this time.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me voice appreciation for the measures being introduced by the government this session. I suppose the proper psychological approach would be to think in terms of a motion of commendation, but I shall reserve that for later in the session.
We welcome amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans Benefit Act, although, as I have already intimated, we do not know to what extent the proposals will go. We would say that to be in any degree satisfactory the requests of the veterans organizations should be acceded to in full. I do not have to go into their requests in detail and place them on record again. They are well known to every hon. member, and I would suggest that the government would be doing the minimum by meeting those requests.
We are also appreciative of the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. However, as other hon, members have stated, there are still many inadequacies quite evident in the legislation. There are still many who should be receiving benefits but who are classed as ineligible. A group of men came to see me several weeks ago and called to my attention the fact that despite their employment with Buckerfield's Limited they were not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. These men might be classed as a marginal group. They are clipper operators and tow truck drivers, and therefore find themselves somewhere in between agricultural workers and those engaged in industry. I submit that in all fairness these men should be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits the same as others who are engaged in operations conducted by Buckerfield's Limited.
The disability pension legislation brought in last session and now proclaimed is wholly commendable but, as has already been stated, it is so restricted in its application that men who should be receiving assistance under the legislation are likewise ineligible.

The Address-Mr. Cannon
We are also appreciative of other things such as the proposal regarding blind pensions and the legislation authorizing loans to fishermen similar to those provided to farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. But again let me say that we are far from satisfied with the situation in regard to the other matters I have mentioned, and I would earnestly request that the attention of the respective departments be called to those problems and something be done to rectify them.

The Address-Mr. Cannon of Quebec, but I read his remarks, and I could hardly believe my eyes when I read them. At page 121 of Hansard the hon. member is reported as having said:
I contend that there is no part ot Canada that is as ripe for advances by the communist party as the province of Quebec.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the greatest exhibition of colossal ignorance that I have ever heard or read in all my life. I would remind the hon. member that apart from the labour progressive party, under which name the communist party masquerades, the party in Canada which is closest to the communist party is the C.C.F.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext: Now who is showing his ignorance?

maintopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND QUESTIONS TO BE DEALT WITH MONDAY, JANUARY 24
speechtext:
Before he talks about there being any danger of the communist party becoming powerful in our province the hon. member had better look to the other provinces where the C.C.F. party is in power or gets a large vote. It is in those provinces that there is a great danger of the communist party taking a foothold, certainly not in the province of Quebec. In Quebec we have respect for constituted authority; we have a true religious sentiment, and there is no danger of the communist party obtaining a foothold in our province. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, in order to illustrate his point, again at page 121 of Hansard is reported to have said:
In the city of Montreal the communist party polled about as many votes as the C.C.F.
In place of saying that the communist party polled about as many votes as did the C.C.F. in the city of Montreal, I think it would be fairer to say that the communist party polled as few votes as did the C.C.F. in the city of Montreal, because the C.C.F. never polled many votes in our province. It has an unblemished record of never having elected a representative in the province of Quebec either to the federal house or to the provincial house.

speechtext:
I wish to turn my attention to the third party of the opposition, namely the Social Credit party. From my county I have been receiving letters cut out from the official newspaper of the Social Credit party in our province, L'Avenir. These letters, which are printed in the newspaper with the caption "Send them to your member", "En-voyez-les a votre depute", are accompanied by bunches of signatures that have been obtained in the constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine by the emissary of the Social Credit party who went down there for that purpose. These letters asked that military expenditures be reduced in order to double family allowances. They contain such demagogic phrases as "Families need more bread than guns to bring up children".
I should like the leader of the Social Credit party to tell the house and the country -because I say the country is entitled to a declaration from the man who is leader of a party that claims to be a national party- whether or not he is in favour of Canadian armament, whether or not he is in favour of Canada living up to the obligations it undertook with the rest of the western European nations to resist communism, whether he is in favour of Canada living up to the obligations that it undertook under NATO. I say that if he is in favour of these things the Social Credit party cannot in good faith tell the people of my county or of any other county that this country ought to reduce military expenditures in order to double family allowances.
I say that if the Social Credit party is in favour of our living up to our obligations under NATO and our obligations to the other free countries allied with us, its leader should denounce in the house and repudiate what has been done in my constituency in the name of the Social Credit party. I shall look forward to hearing him make a statement on that point.

To the people of my constituency I say that first things must come first. If we are to preserve family allowances we have to preserve our liberty and our way of life. The old Roman saying, si vis pacem, para bellum, was never truer than it is today -if you want peace, prepare for war. It is

absolutely necessary that we be strong. Everybody knows that. The leader of the Social Credit party knows it. The emissaries of his party who went to my constituency to try to subvert the people there and make them sign silly petitions know perfectly well, as he and other members of the party here know, that these expenditures must be made. He knows that we have to be strong and that we have to combat communism if we are to retain our way of life and our liberty.
He knows also that our liberty and our way of life are essentials that we must have before we can have any family allowances
The Address-Mr. Cannon at all, let alone double family allowances. I say to the people of my county that when the time comes to increase family allowances the Liberal party will increase them. The Liberal party was the party that introduced family allowances in the first place, and it can be counted upon to increase them when the revenues and wealth of the country permit us to do so.
